title: A Correspondence Between Qubit- and Boson-Based Sensing Protocols
abstract: Recent years have seen a surge of interest in adapting non-classical states to search for physics beyond the Standard Model, including both qubit- and boson-based systems. These two classes of systems are closely related through the Holstein--Primakoff transformation (HPT). In this work, we show that the HPT offers novel insights into inherently quantum-mechanical detection of new physics. We begin by discussing how the HPT can be used to unify certain existing qubit- and boson-based proposals in a single framework. We then show how it naturally reveals a novel generalization of GHZ states which offer superior performance for the detection of rare interactions. We demonstrate that these novel states can be readily prepared, and combine the coherent advantage of GHZ states with superior error rejection. Finally, we show that the HPT also reveals a natural extension of the Hamiltonian-Not-in-Lindblad-Span theorem for collections of bosonic modes.
summary: This paper uses the Holstein-Primakoff transformation to create a unified framework connecting quantum sensing protocols in both bosonic and qubit systems. It demonstrates that this correspondence allows for the construction of superior quantum states and establishes generalized theoretical bounds on sensing precision. The work is significant for guiding the development of next-generation quantum sensors.
main_problem: The paper aims to establish a unified mathematical correspondence between quantum sensing protocols based on bosonic systems and those based on qubit/qudit systems for searching for physics beyond the Standard Model.
main_result: The Holstein-Primakoff transformation (HPT) unifies these protocols, revealing novel generalized GHZ states and extending the Hamiltonian-Not-in-Lindblad-Span theorem for bosonic modes.
method: The core method is the Holstein-Primakoff transformation (HPT), which maps operators and states between the bosonic Fock space and the symmetric qubit Hilbert space.
model_or_system: The study compares two systems: bosonic sensors (e.g., cavities, squeezed light) and qubit/qudit sensors (e.g., trapped atoms, superconducting circuits). The HPT provides the mathematical bridge between them.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information ($F_{	ext{opt}}^Q$), Wigner functions (bosonic and spin), and the achievable scaling of sensitivity bounds.
important_parameters: Number of sensors ($m$), total occupation number ($n$), total spin ($J$), and time ($T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the HPT as a mathematical correspondence and examines specific limiting regimes (e.g., South-Pole or Equatorial limits) for simplification.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Wigner distributions for state mappings, specifically showing the correspondence between the vacuum state and the fully polarized state, and between general Fock states and Dicke states.
paper_structure: The paper reviews the HPT, demonstrates state correspondences (e.g., Fock $\leftrightarrow$ Dicke), discusses sensing implications and scaling analysis, introduces a novel GHZ-4 protocol, and concludes with extensions to the HNLS theorem.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, unifying mathematical tool (HPT) to compare sensing limits across fundamentally different physical platforms (bosons vs. qubits), which is crucial for experimental quantum sensing design.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Wigner distributions for the south-pole state |0⟩⊗N Q of N qubits (left) and for the bosonic vacuum |0⟩B (right); these map to one another under the HPT. The qubit Wigner distribution is approximately gaussian; this is exact on the boson side. We discuss this mapping in Section III A, while Appendix A presents our Wigner function conventions.

FIG. 2. Wigner distributions for the permutation-symmetric, half-up state |J = N/2, M = 0⟩Q of N = 16 qubits (left) and for the bosonic state of 8 photons |N/2⟩B (right); these map to one another under the HPT. Both states have definite excitation numbers, and both Wigner functions exhibit circularly symmetric rings of alternating sign. We discuss this mapping in Section III B, while Appendix A presents our Wigner function conventions.

FIG. 3. Wigner distributions for an example displaced coherent state of qubits (left) and of a bosonic mode (right); these map to one another under the HPT. As in the vacuum (coherent) case, the qubit distribution is approximately gaussian while gaussianity is exact for the bosonic Wigner function. We discuss this mapping in Section III C, while Appendix A presents our Wigner function conventions.

FIG. 4. Wigner distributions for an example spin-squeezed (along Jz) state of qubits (left) and for two types of squeezing of a bosonic mode (right): x quadrature squeezing (upper-right) and number-squeezing (lower-right). The HPT map in this case is somewhat more ambiguous that in the rest of our examples; see the discussion in Sections III D and IV B 3. Appendix A presents our Wigner function conventions.

FIG. 5. Wigner distributions for a qubit GHZ(-2) state aligned with the Jx axis (left) and for a bosonic (2-legged) cat state along the x axis (right); these map to one another under the HPT. For the qubit Wigner function, we additionally include a plot in spherical coordinates (θ, ϕ) to show the entire spherical surface. Both states have two primary lobes at the positions of their component coherent states, as well as interference fringes of alternating sign in between. We discuss this mapping in Section III E, while Appendix A presents our Wigner function conventions.
